messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajiv, a 58-year-old South Asian man and bomb disposal technician, has been struggling with the aftermath of his son’s near-fatal illness. The traumatic event that precipitated Rajiv's current difficulties occurred nearly two years ago when his son was hospitalized for a life-threatening condition. The ordeal left an indelible mark on Rajiv, transforming ordinary sights and smells into potent reminders of that harrowing time. Rajiv’s distress is most acute in settings reminiscent of the hospital—a smell of antiseptic or the sight of medical equipment like needles or drips triggers intense physical reactions and intrusive memories. These triggers are not mere discomforts; they plunge Rajiv back into the fear and helplessness he felt as his son fought for his life. The memory of that time is vivid and overwhelming, often reliving the entire event with a sense of immediacy that leaves him feeling physically and emotionally raw. For instance, while on duty at work, Rajiv was inspecting medical equipment used in bomb disposal simulations. The sight of needles and drips instantly brought back the full memory without warning, leaving him disoriented and shaken. As he relived the experience, he felt the same overwhelming fear and horror, which triggered his sleep vigilance. He found it nearly impossible to fall asleep because he needed to remain alert, as if waiting for another crisis to strike. This cycle of triggers leading to memories further reinforces Rajiv’s negative appraisals. His thoughts that he is a weak person who can't stop bad things from happening to him are exacerbated by these intrusive experiences. He fears that his reactions mean he is going crazy, which only intensifies the sense of threat and vulnerability. The more he believes he is weak, the more vigilant he becomes about potential threats, creating a self-reinforcing loop. Rajiv’s negative appraisals also play a crucial role in how triggers manifest in his daily life. His conviction that he can’t protect his loved ones makes him hypersensitive to any reminder of the hospital environment. The mere thought of being around children heightens his anxiety because it reminds him of the fragility and vulnerability he witnessed during his son’s illness. The narrative of Rajiv's experience is a continuous interplay between these components, where triggers lead to memories, which in turn fuel negative appraisals that reinforce his sense of threat. The cycle feels tightening as each element feeds into the others. For example, when driving past a hospital or encountering medical equipment at work, he experiences an immediate flood of negative emotions and vivid sensory reliving of the event. This not only heightens his physical reactivity but also deepens his belief that he is weak and helpless. The cumulative effect has been profound on Rajiv’s life. His hypervigilance impacts his ability to function effectively at work, where he often finds himself distracted by intrusive thoughts and images. The strain extends into his marriage; his wife notices the increasing distance and tension as Rajiv struggles with these overwhelming feelings. It was a particularly severe episode during a routine check-up for his daughter that finally pushed Rajiv to seek help. He had a full reliving of his son’s illness, which left him feeling physically unwell and emotionally drained. This time, he recognized the futility of trying to manage it alone and was most afraid that these symptoms would continue to worsen without intervention. In seeking psychological assistance, Rajiv hopes for relief from the constant vigilance and intrusive memories. He longs to regain a sense of control over his life and to be able to face reminders of the traumatic event without being overwhelmed by fear and negative self-beliefs.
